title: As above, so below — what it actually means
desc: The most quoted line in esotericism is a 19th-century paraphrase of a medieval Latin sentence from an Arabic text. Here is the real wording — and the real meaning.
h1:
As above, so below:
the autopsy of a quote
tldr: The famous four words are a Victorian-era condensation of a Latin sentence from the Emerald Tablet — a text first attested in Arabic in the 8th–9th century. The original is not a cosmic slogan but a working claim with a purpose clause: the levels of reality answer each other so that the operator can accomplish the work.
body:
You’ve seen it on posters, tattoos and a thousand videos. Today we put the tradition’s most famous sentence on the table and trace where every word actually comes from. This is the path’s first full exercise in our method — and a preview of step 07.

What the source says

The line descends from the Emerald Tablet, whose oldest known home is an Arabic book of secrets from the 8th–9th century. In the medieval Latin vulgate — per the critical edition of Steele & Singer — the sentence runs: Quod est inferius est sicut quod est superius, et quod est superius est sicut quod est inferius, ad preparanda miracula rei unius. In our working translation: “What is below is like what is above, and what is above is like what is below — for preparing the miracles of the one thing.” (Many printed editions since 1541 read ad perpetranda, “for accomplishing” — a genuine variant of the print tradition; the meaning barely shifts, but knowing which text you’re quoting is the whole game on this site.)

Three things the original has that the slogan lost

“Is like”, not “is”. The Latin gives a simile — resemblance between levels, not identity. Both directions. Above mirrors below just as below mirrors above; the traffic runs two ways. A purpose clause. The sentence exists for something: the miracles of the one thing — in context, the alchemical work. This is an operator’s sentence: a claim about why transformation is possible, not a fridge magnet about vibes.

Where the short version came from

The tidy epigram “as above, so below” spread through 19th-century occultism — the era of Blavatsky — as a compression of the Latin. It stuck because it’s beautiful. But compression cut the purpose clause, and with it the meaning drifted: from a thesis grounding a craft to an all-purpose mystical wink.

Is the idea itself Hermetic, then?

Yes — and here honesty cuts our way for once. The intuition behind the line, cosmic sympathy and correspondence, runs genuinely deep in the Corpus and its world: the human as microcosm, heaven mapped onto body and fate. The slogan’s wording is modern; its instinct is ancient. Distinguishing the two is what separates knowing the tradition from quoting it.

Your takeaway sentence

Next time someone tells you “as above, so below” is an ancient Egyptian incantation, you can smile and say: medieval Latin, translating Arabic, compressed by Victorians — and still a better sentence in the original. Step 07 opens the Tablet itself.
facts: Emerald Tablet (first attested in Arabic, 8th–9th c.)
faq: No — it's a compression with a real pedigree. The wording is modern shorthand; the underlying idea of correspondence is ancient. Both facts are true, and both matter.
Does it appear in the Corpus Hermeticum?
Not in this form. The Corpus carries the correspondence idea; the sentence itself belongs to the Emerald Tablet tradition.
Why do you cite two Latin variants?
Because manuscripts and printed editions genuinely differ, and pretending otherwise is how myths start. We quote the critical edition and flag the variant — that's the house method.
sources: Robert Steele & Dorothea Waley Singer, 'The Emerald Table', Proc. Royal Society of Medicine 21 (1928).
